targetAudience.primary: Open-source maintainers and security engineers implementing MCP OAuth clients
targetAudience.knowledgeAssumption: The reader understands OAuth metadata, redirects, callbacks, state and PKCE.
targetAudience.readerProblem: A client can accept syntactically valid metadata or callbacks from the wrong authorization server because location is mistaken for identity.

whyNow: Two independent maintainer changes in the MCP Python SDK and Gemini CLI converged on issuer binding at different occurrences while exposing different comparison semantics.

externalHook.description: A valid URL and well-formed response can still belong to an authorization server the client did not intend to trust.

coreProposition: MCP OAuth clients should select expected issuer identity before following discovery indirection, bind every authority-bearing artifact and response to it, and fail closed on mismatch or downgrade; discovery location must not redefine credential authority.

originalValue.description: Unifies metadata and callback fixes into an occurrence-complete issuer-binding rule and identifies comparison semantics as an interoperability boundary.

readerTakeaway: Choose expected issuer identity before discovery; bind metadata, token construction and callbacks to it; invalidate state and fail closed on mismatch, with explicit lower-assurance compatibility modes.

supported: The Python SDK validates discovered authorization-server metadata and token construction against expected issuer.
Gemini CLI validates RFC 9207 issuer at the local callback and rejects missing or mismatched values when expected.
The two implementations use different observed issuer comparison semantics.
unsupported: A complete interoperable profile across MCP clients
Protection without TLS, state, PKCE or audience binding
uncertain: Safe token-cache migration across issuer changes

firstPartyRole.rationale: The argument compares general open-source protocol implementations.

decisionReason: Independent implementations address the same authority-confusion class at complementary protocol occurrences and expose a concrete interoperability gap.
